Did Miss Todd accompany herself while she played and sang, or did you other instruments count?
She played in a comedy herself. She played, well we all played in there with her, you see.
Well tell me, did she sing in what we today would call the jazzy or bluesy style, or was it pretty straight?
Well it was pretty straight. But you know she could always make the people like it somehow or other.
Well this was years before Bessie Smith came along, wasn't it? Bessie Smith, let's see, was what she was... What year was that she was? Flourishing around 1926, 1926.
Oh, that was after us. That was after our time.
When was this that Miss Todd was singing?
All the way from 1913 to 1925. And that was a good ten to twelve years before Bessie was
alive. That's right, from 1913. She didn't sing blues? Well, huh? Or did she?

No, we didn't have, we didn't sing no blues. Well we played the blues but we didn't sing. You didn't sing, not those words. When we were playing at Tom Anderson though, we used to have a special fellow there, especially to sing. And every now and then he'd sing a song or two.
Did he, did Mr. Anderson hire him himself or did the director of the band?
No, no, Mr. Anderson hired him himself. Who was that? I bet I know. Oh, let me see what's new that fellow again.
He's from New Orleans?
Yeah, a little fellow from New Orleans. Colored Boy? Yeah, Colored Boy.
Went to New York?
I don't know what name, you name them, maybe I might think of his name.
Well I would say-
As good as I know his name I just can't think of it right now.
Well I'm going to be leading, but I would lead you into the question, but I would say Willie Jackson, huh?
That's it, that's it.
He ain't his partner, he had a partner, Nookie Johnson and Willie Jackson.
Yeah, he used to sing, that boy could sing, I used to like him singing.
He made some records with Steve and Steve could play. He may not be unable to read, but Steve could play that piano, Steve Lewis.
Did he play that piano? That was Pierrot's piano player. You have to hit off. Oh, God. He's still living?
Who's Steve? Oh no, he died. Oh no. Yes, indeed.
That was Pierrot's piano player. That's why I feel that was the only weak part Pierrot had. That was his weak spot. Pierrot had a good band though. They went to New York and had records.
They did.

That's why I took that dinner dance over at the North Country Club. Outside that I used to play the dinner dance. But I didn't play the afternoon tea dance, you see, because they didn't want no blowing instrument there.
They want quieter music, huh?
Do you want, you know, I used that as a joke. But wouldn't you believe I was the only fellow in the North Country Club and played afternoon tea?
Is that right? That was real high class.
I have to laugh, but you know, you're open using the North Country Club, can tell you.
They just didn't quite have the class.
How do you think I did it? Wow. It was peculiar how I done that, because you see, I was the leader of the band. Yeah. See? And they didn't want no blowing instrument there.
So you got a stick?
But I got in there. You don't know how I got in there.
With a baton, huh?

No. Yeah. It was peculiar the way I got in there. You see, the lady that I'm telling you all about, Miss Todd, she sang. You see? And those people would be sitting down eating, you understand? And I told her, I said, Chick, I used to call her Chick, you know, I said, Chick, you know what do we do? Let's play another selection. Nice selection. You see? And I'll take that horn, you understand? And I could play that horn. You could be sitting down there, you could always hear it.
Just somehow. Did you use your mute or just soften it?

No, just soften it like that. Then I used the mute afterwards, you see? Chick, play that selection, you understand? Because they're all sitting down eating, you see? And me, I stood there a long time, you know, and every now and then I'd come in there, you see? Yeah. Every now and then I'd come in there. Do you know when we got through playing that selection, those people looked like they went wild? They did. That's right. Do you know I stood in there until I got sick and couldn't play no more?
Is that right?
That's right. I had to laugh. I said, that Pierrot got a fine band and I said, he can't have no horn in there. And I said, look me, I'm going in there and play my horn. That's right.
Did those people come up and tell you the numbers they wanted you to play? Sometimes. Sometimes they would.
What would you play? What number?
Well, it all depends what they wanted, you see. Mm-hmm.
Did they, they wanted usually the quieter things, gradually did they like the louder things?

Nope. Not when the afternoon tea. Afternoon tea, you could hear a pin drop on that flute. Oh yeah, because it was all them old people, you know, sitting down here, you see. That dinner dance, all right at night, you understand, we used to step on it then. But that afternoon tea, that's them big rich guys, they're all sitting down there, you see. And every now and then one would get up and make a dance, you see. And I'm telling you,
let me see. What did I play anyway? Did you play any of these waltzes from Europe, any of those things like this? Mazurka, Charlizey, Pulpah?
That sounds like the rosary. The rosary. That's just the thing I played there. I
want those people just like that. Can you beat that? Well of course that was tremendously popular. That was tremendously popular. And you know, that horn looked like,

you know, it's like if you was in the woods, you know. You know, that man still could play that funk before he's singing that. When we got through, I'm telling you, those people, bah bah bah bah bah bah bah bah bah. I told Chick, I said Chick, I got him. Will your doctor let you play anymore? Well he didn't stop me because I had to stop. You see, on the last day, you see the doctor tried to stop me but he couldn't. You see they had me to go to Dr. Hava in the Chicka building on Canal Street where I got Chauveti's place now. Well Dr. Hava was one of the finest positions you had in the city of New York. And those people did everything possible to see that I would get well, you see. But when I'd blow that instrument, it looked like if you'd take a razor, you know, and cut right here. And you know how that happened? I couldn't sleep in the daytime and I used to play day and night. Oh and this was in the nerves. That's right. The nerves acting up. They claimed that it was weeks planned right here. And the doctor said they never knew of anybody who lived with that. Is that right? But believe me, I got frightened only once, the whole time I was sick. I went to an insurance business after I left the music. And on my route, when I got on Dupree and Broad, they had one of my insurer there. He used to work for the New Orleans Railway Light Company, one of the porters there. And he was giving me the same symptom that I had, you see. And the next day when I went to collect there again, they had unburied him. So you just started taking care of yourself. But I was praying to the Blessed Mother, I said, let me get away from God. I'll never put that in my lip no more.
Oh my. Well who plays the piano? Who has? Here, you've got a piano.
Oh yeah. I used to like the piano. I used to kind of bang on that myself sometimes. Then sometimes I had to kind of help out. You really did. Maybe we could get a little
something. Do you still play for yourself at all? Not at all now? No, no. Touching.

What numbers would you play on the piano? Well, one or two different little numbers. I used to play like that just for past time. You have children? No ma'am. I raised a daughter though. She was here last,
she's the one that was in Philadelphia. In California.
Yeah. California. She's back now. She's in New Orleans now.
Oh man. What were the numbers you played on the piano? Can you tell me the names?
Oh well, it was a different one. Let me see.
They've got some numbers you can't tell in front of ladies. Really?
It looked like since I got away from that I guess.
You can't remember them now. Tell them about the Red Book. I bet none of them know about the Red Book.
Well, let me tell you one thing. We were the only one who could cut the Red Books. Mm-hmm. Cut Joplin music you're talking about. Yeah. What was that time? We were the only one.
At the right time.
That was right time.
Yes, that's right.
That tempo you played that fast?
We could play that baby. Well you know this interests me because I mean now so then not only then did you have your right time on the piano but you played this on your trumpet and other-
That's right. That's why I used to play it on the trumpet.
Well I'll be there.
The lady that I'm telling you about, she played it on the piano. Yeah. Camilla Todd? Oh yeah. Camilla could play anything you could play.
She's still living in New Orleans.
Oh no, she's still teaching too. I might have seen her before I went to New York because her brother, he's a musician.
Have you been to see her and gotten a record on her? I don't know where to find the exam.
Oh sure. You know where that Baptist church on Magnolia and Louisiana Avenue? Mm-hmm. That red brick building, that a Baptist church on the corner?
That's where they buried Celestan from.
Well that's right, that's right. Well right in the back. Was Papa Celestan a Baptist?
Sure. He was everything.
He was everything. Celestan was a Mason, he was a Masonic, he was an art father. Knives of Columbus.
No, he was Catholic too.
No, no, he wasn't. Oh no.
I got it wrong, the Knights of St. Peter Clay were out of here.
No, no, uh-uh. No, no, no, I wasn't Knight of St. Peter Clay. No, no, he was an art father. Celestan was an art fella, Masonic, and a piece. He was. That's right. That's how you got to get a job.
That's how you used to get all those jobs. Oh well that's pretty good, that's a good business.

And that's how it come to kill me too. That's all, because if I didn't play with him, those funerals I had to play with Mr. Moret, that was the excelsior. Because manual parade wasn't there, this fella wasn't there, that fella wasn't there, in other words he didn't have no musician in Syrman, they were always there. And so all those parade and funerals, it was he polite, Charles.
Can you think that's it?

And that's why I made my mistake. I wouldn't refuse Mr. Moret because he'd get hot. I wouldn't refuse Celestan because he'd get hot. So therefore when one didn't have it, the other one had it, you see. But I had to play with them, both of them. And then playing my Knight work, every night, every night, every night, no night off.
Tell me this, what happened when the Navy closed up Storyville? What did most of the musicians do? Did they still have enough jobs to play around that?

No they didn't. When did they go? There were a few, Celestan had the Beverly Garden over at Jack Sheen, Piron had Tranchino over at West End, we had Moulin Rouge, I mean the Spanish fort was Piron, Moulin Rouge was also at the West End, Du Bois at the West End. Besides that all the rest of the place was closed, you see. And so the musicians had to pick up the best way they could. Sometimes
some of them didn't play for a month. And that's why some of them, so many, went north, because they closed Storyville in what, 1918?
It looked like to me. That was closed before then, eh?
First World War.
It was closed several times.

It was closed. Now you see, you get to the Gyp the Blood killing. You remember the Gyp the Blood killing? I heard about it. Well that was about 1913, wasn't it, I think, you know. My teacher, Manuel Moneta, was playing.
Manuel was still playing?
He was playing across the street. Yeah, Manuel still plays piano.
Oh yeah.

But that reminds me, we forgot about accordion. But anyway, he was playing right across the street I think from where the murder was, you know. Harry Parker, Charlie Parker, Billy Phillips, Gyp the Blood, they had a terrible killer in there and they closed down that town. So you know, that slowed things down. Well how many places did they close down when they closed down that had actual
bands? Because I think it was around 17, 1916 and 17 they closed this place.

Well they did it a couple times. World War I. No, but this was permanent. Yeah, that was in 1917. Yeah. Mr. Charles, we wanted to ask you about the use of the accordion in these jazz groups that you played with. When did you use it?

Well I used that, not me, but the bands I played with. Like Parence, let me see who was that band. I'm trying to think who was that band. But I used to probably a fellow by the name of Billy Phillips used to play that accordion. And I mean he sure would play that accordion.
But you didn't use it much then?
No, very, very seldom. Very seldom. In other words they didn't use accordion at all those things.
What about Peyton? Do you remember him?
I heard talk of him. I never met him. He was accordion prior. I can't remember too many of them.
What other instruments, unusual instruments, got into those combos down there beside the
accordion? Can you remember any others? What about piccolo?

Piccolo. We didn't have that. Very few people could play piccolo over there. Who were there? Who were the ones who could? Let me see which one I could think of playing piccolo. I can't think of who I could play that piccolo. I know I've seen some played already. I knew just like I've seen some played here. You never worked with Bab Frank? I'm glad you mentioned his name. I knew I had played with piccolo already. Yeah, Bab Frank. That's a little bit of sort of a red looking color. I never knew him, but I used to hear fest
when I ever talk about him playing, beating all the guys. Did he play in dance bands?

Oh yeah, in dance bands. What kind of part would he play? Piccolo. Piccolo part. They had it written out for him on everything. I suppose so, because he didn't play with us, you see. But I played with band that he would play.

Did he play most of the way through a number or did he just have certain places to play? No, he played through a number. Did the saxophones come in with the jazz combos from the very beginning or were they added later on? You said the saxophone come in later on,

yeah, that's right, because we used to use clarinet. And then the clarinet player took it. Then they double up on second clarinet. But the clarinet was the main one. All those bands was using when I went into the city of New Orleans, from 19, I'm sure from 1909 up until 1916, that's all they were using, clarinet. Then they began to use saxophone, because I've used saxophone myself. The same fellow you see I got in that picture there, he played saxophone also.
You mean Sam Dutry? Sam Dutry.

Did the musicians, I had already asked if you used any Cajun folk songs from this area, you said no. Were there any musicians from Latin America, you know, South America, that came in there that at any time that your group heard play or that played with you, that would give you any, say, Latin rhythms? Do you recall any kind of music of this kind being used?

You didn't play any rhombos? No. Well we played rhombos. You did? We just, you know, from the music. And then we put on whatever part we wanted in there, you see. But we played rhombos and music. In other words we played all kinds of music. Couldn't name a piece of music that we didn't play.
What would be the head numbers you'd play?
Well anything we could think of that we picked up from hearing the other fellow play.
Well I mean did people want to come up and hear those low down, you know, real gut bucket numbers?
The whole blues? If you didn't play the blues you didn't play nothing. So who? Oh my goodness. For everybody. It looked like they just liked that blues business.
You mean you even played it at the country club?
Well I certainly.
Well I have more use for the jukebox than I have.
Blues. They like it everywhere. All kinds of people like blues.
Blues? That's the thing people like. Not T for Two and all that kind of stuff, Whiskpring and Avalon and all that kind of stuff.

I wanted to ask you something. I've been curious about this for a long time. What did the customers do when they came into Storyville and listened to this music? What did you men do? Were you just over some side and these women that were there and these men, did they stay somewhere else? Did they applaud? Did they do anything at all?
They did applaud. Believe me you start playing and they stay right there until you stop playing. Is that right? Oh my goodness.
When they applauded a number what did you do?
You played again. I bet you'd be too glad to play it again because I'm supposed to put the hand in their pocket and try to start throwing that money on the floor. I'm not sure.
So when they applaud you always play the same number.

You know how much they was paying to play there? One dollar a night. Man of mine, he's going to tell you, Peter Bocaz, young girl can tell you. Because me, I wasn't playing regular there. I mean I used to go play like that in one another's place. Because like I'm telling you, I'm sorry I didn't go play there because if I was like where I lived, today I would be pretty well fixed up. Who were they? Oh yes indeed. Because those men used to come off the ship, come throw money on the floor just like if you were throwing corn.
What's the biggest night you ever had for tips? Do you remember?

Oh, by the thirteen dollars. But you know Peter Owen and Celestine? Celestine ought to die rich man. That's the man ought to die rich man. He was making house thirty-five, forty dollars a night over that jack sheep. And me when I went down one night and Celestine's place only made nine dollars. I said it just wasn't my luck to play for those places. I used to like to play, you know.
Thirty-five dollars in tips?
Why sure, thirty-five dollars a night. For one man? Hmm, that's good money.
Well now, and they would come up there.

Ask people what them fellas used to do at those different places. Some nights they used to make money like, oh my goodness. Oh, the spell come off the ship, throw money on the floor, I'm telling you, just like you're throwing corn on the floor.
Well why did you play in the district? I didn't play that much, no, don't forget.

I know you weren't playing. Oh, oh, oh. I tell you I got a beating for that. I mean a good win for that. Yes, indeed. I went and played at the place they used to call Alozo's in New Iberia. I was quite a lad. I was only fifteen years old. And when I came here, somebody went there with my cousin, and somebody told my father that I played in Napoleon's place, he said, where at? They said, Alozo's. What was you doing in Alozo? I said, well I didn't know any better, I just went there with my cousin Richard. And everybody said, all right, come on over here. Next time you go to New Iberia, you don't go to those places, you ain't got no business there. And believe me, I was afraid of

those places from that day on. Tell me, did you notice in the people that you associated with sort of an attitude of looking down their nose at you because you were a jazz player, did you meet any of that at all in New Orleans? Well that's good. I'm glad they didn't. I know in North Louisiana, how I was raised in a very strict Protestant atmosphere. All of this was looked upon as being highly sinful and so on, you know. And so we had to skirt around the edge of jazz for a long

time, you know. You're from around Shreveport? Yes, north of Shreveport. Well, I played over there because you were in a roof garden for a whole summer, for Mr. Ballantyne. Sure. He came and got me, I was playing that tomass in there. That's right. That's right. A whole summer I played that. Oh but that was one of the best roof garden jobs I ever had. Oh that was a nice place. Oh, we used to live at Dr. King's house on Douglas Street. I used to go to, on Sundays I used to go to the Protestant church. They had a Catholic church there but I don't think they had a handful of

people there. Oh, in those days there were relatively few Catholics there. That's right. That's right. Did they have any jazzy piano playing and jazzy music at the Protestant church you attended? No. Well I was raised up, for instance, going to both white churches and also Negro churches up there. They had some very gut-buckety piano playing, you know, rather goofy piano playing in the churches. There was one girl who, named Jewel Webb, who had learned it from listening to the records of the Economist who played for Bessie Smith. And when she went to the Baptist church in Mansfield, the second Baptist church, I was saying, oh Mansfield, boy you really heard some down-to-earth piano playing in those Protestant hymns. Is there anything that you have neglected on this thing here?

Yeah, I forgot to tell you hello from below, Bonds. Remember the saxophone player which I left there? I met him on the street and he said to be sure and tell you hello. Oh, tell him the same for me. I will. I wanted to ask you about saxophone there. You remember him, huh? Yeah. Mealy Barnes, his little brother? His little brother, Mealy's little brother. But anyway, who was the first one to play a saxophone in New Orleans that you heard then?
Hmm. Oh, it's hard to say all now because it looked like when one picked it up the whole bunch started playing. Yeah.
All of a sudden. Well who started the fast thing right on the saxophones?

Because you take a fellow like Louis, he never did play nothing but that clarinet. No, he wasn't. But you take Tio, Tio had a saxophone, take Sam Dutrae, this fellow there, he had a saxophone. And who else? Two or three.
John Joseph had one early, huh? You remember that?
Oh yeah, John Joseph. I remember the Joseph.
He's still playing. He's only 85. Huh? No, he's still. 86. He's still here. He still plays bass in New Orleans. Oh, I see. Cuts hair by day and plays bass at night. Wasn't he a president?
No, and Willie Joseph. Where is he at? He's the one that should be playing that saxophone.
He passed. He passed. He passed. He was hit by a car, hit one driver. Came back from California to visit his brothers and got one of them. He was a pastor. Palleter you're talking about.
Willie I used to call him. He played with us too already. But he didn't play saxophone then, he was playing clarinet. With who? Which band? With the Silver Leaf band. There's a band right there.
Oh yeah. Did he play before Dutri?

But no. Substitute. Substitute, that's right. For instance, Dupre couldn't play, you see. Whenever he couldn't play with this fellow, we hired anybody who we couldn't get. That's the way, that's how I come to play with some of that fellow you were talking about playing that piccolo.
Was it Willie Joseph?
Bad Frank, yeah. That was his name, Bad Frank. I remember that.
What about Willie Joseph? Was he a good reader or would he be mostly an ear man or what?

Not fancy. But this fellow right there, he was a good reader. He was the one who used to arrange all our music. You see, for instance, you want a number and we didn't have the orchestration of the number. Well we used to have to have somebody to buy a piano copy, you see. And this fellow is the one who used to do all the arranging. Oh, good. Did he do much of this for you? Oh yeah. All the music that we had to arrange, he's the one that arranged.
Did you pay him extra for this? No. He was glad to do it.
Well, well. Oh yeah. It was very cooperative. He couldn't have no, didn't have no trouble with
those men and yards. There were not a lot of arrangers there though, huh? No. Not too many guys who could arrange. No, no, no. Oh, when was the... There was only three of them. Him,
old man Cousteau, and somebody else. Besides that, there's no other one there. You were a trumpeter. Cousteau? Yeah, old man Cousteau, yeah.

Would that be Emmanuel Cousteau's father? No, I don't know. You know him? Well I guess he's after your time. I think he was born in 1918 or something like that. I heard him the other night, the young Cousteau is playing progressive jazz now. We heard him the other night with a big band. He was playing with the Royal Dukes of Rhythm now.
Because old man Cousteau, he used to arrange a little bit, not much. Which one? This fellow was a good arranger.
Which Cousteau is this? I don't understand. That's Louis, Louis Cousteau.
Is there a possibility that these arrangements which they made are still in the hands of some of these men or their families in your audience?
I wonder. That's what that's... It would certainly be interesting to get your hands on, Dick.
Well we got, we got, we bought the Rovershaw collection.
You did? You got the Rovershaw collection.
We just bought that the other day.
Well I'm sure you must have some arrangements.
There's some arrangements and there must be about 5,000 pieces in there. 5,000 arrangements. And we got it cheap too.

Oh yeah, oh well yeah, they have no use for it. No, no, the man was bad. I wish I could think about where some of my numbers are, but I couldn't think. And I used to, because I had the case on my hand.
Well if you do locate him at those, be sure to let him know. Oh, I'm sure.

You see, like I said, after I gave up that instrument, it looked like I'd never go back to it no more. I just simply gave all I could away and what I didn't give away, I burned it up and things like that. Because I never once thought that I'd ever go back to music. You ought to go to school all the time. I was 19, I was 19 long years in that business.
Yeah.
Thank you.

Let's see. This is Hippolyte Charles, Real Three, April the 13th, 1963. I guess about an hour ago we were talking about the Vidals, and I never did get who they were. Who were the Vidals? They were the little band.

They had Louis Vidal, Tom Vidal, and Pierre Vidal, and Gilles Dey. There was four pieces. And you don't realize the music that those fellas could perform. All blowing instruments too. Louis played trombone, Gilles Dey played trumpet, Tom played trumpet, and Pierre, he played the bass. I'm telling you, you couldn't keep quiet when they started playing that jazz. There was four pieces. And all Louis could come in there so nice with his trombone, I'm telling you it was beautiful. And they played nice and soft. They didn't play that whole loud stuff.
Well that's the first time I'd ever heard of it. You mean the jazz but a muted kind of jazz.
Oh yes indeed. We didn't play that hard stuff either. We played, but I'm telling you, a good rhythm.
All reading or some faking or what? Oh. Some by ear?

Some faking and some, but we used to fake them, many times we used to fake them. Just fake them like that, just put anything we wanted. Would you believe I have never seen the music of the blues? Is that right? And ask me how many times I don't play the blues.
I have never seen music of the blues.

I've seen music of the St. Louis blues, because that was handed. I've seen music of the, what do you call it, Wabash blues. I've seen music of another blues I know. Two or three other blues I know. But that old down blues that we used to play, I've never seen the music of that.
Maybe nobody ever wrote it down. Maybe it was always played by the head. So some things get passed on that way you know.

Because some of them fellas used to come holler, you understand? Play that blues, so and so, play that blues. And then I just, ta ta dee, ta ta dee, ta ta dee, ta ta da da. Just like that. You see I knew like the tune. We played the tune. But I've never seen no music of that.

I was reading about the first time that Hande performed his blues in the song. One of the clubs in Memphis. They said, my goodness when he hit that thing. Boy, and gave a few, I mean that rhythm, set up that blues rhythm and so on. They said those people went wow.

But you know his blues wasn't like that old down blues. You said? No. No, not the real. His blues, ta da dee dee, ta da da dee dee, ta da da dee dee, you see? Yes. Then ta da da dum, ta da dum, ta da dum, you know? That's right. But not this down blues. Uh huh. These down blues go, ta da dee, ta da dee, ta da dee da da da da da dee, da da. You see? That old down blues go. And then you could compose it, put anything you want in it, you see? You could even put, ta da da da da da da da da da da da da da da da da da da da da da. You see? That old down blues go. Yeah. And then you could compose it, put anything you want in it, you see? You could even put, ta da da da da da da da da da da da da da da da. You see? Put, we'll just bring that in there. But that wasn't that old, that wasn't the real blues itself. But that old blues, like I'm telling you, that's the old blues. That's the way you used to play that thing. And believe me, when you'd hear that old trombone in there, you'd have to move up too.
What was the first band you heard when you went to New Orleans? Did you go as a kid before you moved out? Oh no.

When I first went to New Orleans I went to study music. That was your first time? Oh yeah. That was my first time in New Orleans. In 1909 I went to study music. And I was taking lessons from Mr. Moret on Ursuline Street. Which one? Eugene. That's the one who used to play with only white bands. Never played with colored bands. His brother is the one, George Moret, that's the one who used to have the excelsior band.
His wife is still alive, George's wife. That's what young Louis Cattrall told me, the clarinet play. Oh yes, I see. Well his daddy used to play with me.
He was one of our best drummers. He could read some music, let me tell you.
But Eugene Moret played only with white bands, no? No.
Oh yeah, Eugene, yeah. But not George. George played with colored bands.
Well what color was George? Was he real bright? That's funny.

One of them was, we call it a briquet, you know what I mean, the red. Yeah. See? And the other one was dark-complected with black, black hair. That's George? That's the one I used to take music lessons from, the one with the dark-complected with black, black hair. He lived in Bay St. Louis.
That's Eugene Moret.
Well that's really something.
But then the same family.
The same family. Two brothers.
The light one wouldn't pass.
The light one didn't pass and the dark one passed. But you couldn't tell him from a nation.
You couldn't tell him from a nation? That's right.
Just like a Mexican, you couldn't tell the difference.
I'll tell you that's remarkable.
